flawed_step: The universal claim fails: being 3-connected and claw-free does not force a Hamiltonian cycle. The Matthews–Sumner conjecture asks for 4-connectivity.
counterexample: The truncated Petersen graph T(P): replace each vertex v of the Petersen graph by a triangle on the pairs (v,e), e incident to v, and join (u,uv) to (v,uv). It is cubic with 30 vertices. Claw-free: each vertex's two neighbours inside its triangle are adjacent. 3-connected: the symmetry group of P is transitive on (vertex, incident edge) pairs, so T(P) is a connected vertex-transitive cubic graph, and Watkins–Mader gives connectivity > 2*3/3 = 2, hence 3. Not Hamiltonian: a Hamiltonian cycle must use exactly 2 of each triangle's 3 outgoing edges. Using 0 closes a 3-cycle; using 1 or 3 makes the degree sum inside the triangle odd. Shrinking the triangles then gives a Hamiltonian cycle of the Petersen graph, which does not exist.
assessment_summary: Counterexample: the truncated Petersen graph (30 vertices, cubic). It is claw-free because every vertex sits in a triangle, and 3-connected because it is a connected vertex-transitive cubic graph. A Hamiltonian cycle would have to use exactly two outgoing edges per triangle, which would give a Hamiltonian cycle of the Petersen graph, and there is none. So the statement is false.
